# Chapter 4 — sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) The hardware is worth a few hundred kroner and is easily replaced; the
customer data on it can expose customers, trigger GDPR duties and destroy trust.
The loss is therefore valued by what the information's exposure would cost the
business, not by the replacement price of the machine. (2) Product catalogue:
Availability dominates (it is meant to be seen) --- protected by capacity and
resilience. Order records: Integrity dominates (they must be right) ---
protected by access control and logging of changes. Checkout: Availability
dominates (revenue stops without it) --- protected by denial-of-service defences
and redundancy. (3) Requiring MFA closes the vulnerability, so the likelihood of
account takeover falls sharply and the risk shrinks --- but the hacker and the
credential-stuffing attempts are still out there, so the threat is unchanged.
Risk lives in the meeting of the two, which is why both the weaknesses and the
threat picture are managed. (4) Threat acts: An attacker sends the phishing
email --- intervene with filtering and awareness training. Exploits a
vulnerability: The attachment runs and the staff member's machine is unprotected
--- intervene by patching and hardening. Causes an incident: Ransomware encrypts
the data --- intervene by detecting and isolating early. Leading to impact: The
checkout is down and data may be exposed --- intervene with backups, a response
plan and notification. (5) Supplier price lists: Internal --- staff need them,
leakage causes minor commercial harm; handling rule: Staff-only access, not
published. Customer database: Confidential --- personal data whose disclosure
causes real harm (R3); handling rule: Encrypted storage with strictly limited
access and careful disposal.
